title: The Witch, The Goat, and The Moonpetal Bloom
markdown:
The Whispering Peaks were a place of winding paths that coiled like sleepy snakes, and hidden pools that mirrored the sky like fallen stars. Tucked into the mountainside, little slate-roof villages sat cozy as a hen’s nest. In a small cottage between old pines that whispered secrets to the wind lived Witch Hazel. She was not the sort to cackle or zoom on a broom. You were more likely to find her fussing over the herb garden, brow a little crinkled, or brewing a strong cup of nettle tea that tasted of sunshine and good intentions. Her dearest friend, always near, was Lentil: a small round hedgehog with a twitchy nose and prickles that could tell a whole story of his feelings. He was never far from her side.

A blustery morning. Wind used the chimney as an instrument. Hazel’s spectacles slipped. “Elder Willow does not look happy. I promised a Moonpetal before sundown, and the petals are only now thinking about it.” Apron brushed. “Come, Lentil. Quiet adventure.” A snuffle; a shiver that might have been excitement or breeze.

They started in a robin-cheerful hum, basket on her shoulder, his legs a blur. Higher up, the mountain grew playful. A gust nearly sent the hat into a ditch. Moss that had been carpet became puddle; she wobbled. “A bit lively today.” Lentil’s ankle-nudge was a small reassurance. Then the map — treasured parchment, quickest way to the Glade — was not in the basket. “Acorns. Where has it gone?”

A grey-and-white streak: Bartholomew the goat, famous for leaps and for anything that crunched, map proud in his mouth. He did not mean trouble. Maps were delightfully chewy. “Not for eating!” Lentil squeaked the same news in hedgehog.

As the goat took a rocky ledge, a voice bright as stream-water called, “Lost something?” A young wizard on a boulder, twelve or so, ginger mop, mischief in the sparkle. Pip of the Emerald Valley, still learning to keep enthusiastic spells in the pen, heart usually in the right field. “I saw him take it. He does that. I’m Pip. Can I help?”

Hazel looked him over, practical. “A wizard. Timing’s useful. Catch Bartholomew, or find the Glade without the chew-toy.”

Pip puffed. “Lumen is good in tricky spots. I can do stars, though the clouds are shy.”

They climbed: stony slopes, narrow ledges, a soft glowing orb floating ahead. Bartholomew, a clever climber, drew them higher, air thinner, mist thicker, to a dark cave mouth, and in he went to gnaw in private.

“Oh dear.” Lentil huffed determination. Pip said, “Wait,” stepped in, and Lumen bloomed — not the gentle orb but a brighter ancient pour, moonlight from a pitcher. The cave was a secret library: scrolls, dusty books. On a high shelf, two emerald cat’s eyes blinked like jewels. A midnight cat stretched. Bartholomew, startled, dropped the map. The cat’s tail flicked it toward Pip.

Mostly in one piece, a little nibbled. “Looking for a good story,” Pip giggled. Hazel took the parchment, competence returning. “Hurry.” Bartholomew sniffed a scroll as if considering a second course. They emerged. Pip focused the beam; Hazel and the restored map found the bearing; Lentil scurried, prickles on purpose.

They arrived just as the last rays painted the sky rose and gold. In the sheltered glade the Moonpetals unfurled their silvery blossoms, releasing a faint sweet perfume that made Lentil’s nose work overtime. Hazel carefully gathered a bloom, petals cool and smooth against her fingers. Bartholomew, having decided libraries were a bit too quiet for his taste, ambled up looking rather sheepish. She smiled and patted his sturdy flank. “No harm done. You did lead us here, after all.”

Elder Willow took the bloom at the roots. Leaves rustled as if something had drunk. A warmth moved in the trunk. A soft voice, almost leaf: “You kept your promise.” Hazel scratched Lentil. Pip beamed about goats and libraries. They walked down under a sky beginning to speckle. The path, no longer contrary, felt like a path again. Hazel did not boast, or ask the trees to file the tale. The basket held one stem and a map with teeth-marks, which was, she thought, an accurate record of the day.
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing mountain fantasy adventure for older children
